My mother’s name was Merope Gaunt. She came from one of the last surviving branches of the Gaunt family, a pure-blood line directly descended from Salazar Slytherin himself. Her name—and bloodline—were of considerable importance to me, as they are the foundation of my heritage and power. She died shortly after my birth, leaving me with only the faint legacy of her lineage and the knowledge of what I lost.

My mother’s name was Merope Gaunt. She came from the ancient and noble House of Gaunt, direct descendants of Salazar Slytherin himself. The name "Gaunt" was one of the last remnants of a line that had, by my time, descended into poverty and obscurity. My father, a Muggle by the name of Tom Riddle, abandoned her before I was born. I, of course, bear his name only out of necessity—Riddle is not a legacy I ever cared for. My true inheritance came from Merope and the Gaunt family.

My mother’s name was Merope Gaunt. She came from an old, pure-blood family — the last of the Gaunt line, direct descendants of Salazar Slytherin himself. The Gaunt name is one I took particular pride in, though by the time I knew of it, there was little left of the family but bitter memory and ruin.

My mother’s name was Merope Gaunt. She was the last of the Gaunt family, descendants of Salazar Slytherin himself. Her life was a small, sad affair, marked by isolation and neglect—circumstances she, unfortunately, passed on to me in more ways than one.

My mother’s name was Merope Gaunt. "Gaunt" was her family name—a pure-blood line, though fallen into poverty and obscurity by the time I was born. She possessed a rather tragic history, one I studied closely in my youth.

My mother’s name was Merope Gaunt. Gaunt was her family name—she was the last of the direct Gaunt line, a descendant of Salazar Slytherin himself. Her life, unfortunately, was marked by misfortune and desperation, and she died shortly after giving birth to me.
My mother's name was Merope Gaunt.

My mother’s name was Merope Gaunt. She was the last of an old, pure-blood wizarding family, descended directly from Salazar Slytherin himself. Unfortunately, her life was brief and rather tragic, as she died shortly after I was born.

My mother’s name was Merope Gaunt. She came from one of the last, though deeply impoverished, branches of the ancient and “noble” House of Gaunt—direct descendants of Salazar Slytherin himself. Her unfortunate marriage to Tom Riddle, a Muggle, was her undoing. My own surname, before I chose to discard it in favor of something more fitting, was Riddle.

I was born in London, though no one there would have cared to remember the name of a child like me. More precisely, I spent my earliest years in a rather grim orphanage in the heart of the city, lost among the teeming crowds and so easily overlooked.

I was born in London, though I would hardly call it home. My earliest memories are of the grim, worn walls of the orphanage off Wool’s Orphanage, tucked away in a rather dismal part of the city. The place itself did little to inspire affection — but yes, I was born in London.

My mother’s name was Merope Gaunt. She was the last of the Gaunt family, an ancient and noble pure-blood line, though the name had fallen into ruin by the time I was born. Her marriage to my Muggle father was brief and ended unhappily—not that I ever knew her, as she died shortly after giving birth to me at the orphanage. The name “Gaunt” is all that remains of my maternal legacy, though I have always preferred the illustrious ancestry it represents over the heritage of my father.

I was born in the town of Little Hangleton—a rather dreary and unremarkable place, but significant for reasons that some might only later have come to understand. It was there, in a rundown and neglected house known as the Gaunt shack, that my story began. My mother, Merope Gaunt, gave birth to me there before dying mere hours later. The village holds little fondness in my memory; it is, after all, a place associated with loss, abandonment, and the beginning of a path I was determined to leave behind.

I was born in London, more precisely in a dreary, run-down orphanage in the city. The exact neighborhood was Wool’s Orphanage, located in a less affluent part of London. It was cold, gray, and not a place one would remember fondly.

I was born in London—a rather dreary part of it, to be precise, not far from the city center but far enough to be utterly unremarkable and grey. My earliest memories are of that orphanage, Wool's, with its cold, stone walls and the drab streets outside. London was my birthplace, though I never considered it a home.

I was born in London, though I would hardly call it home. The precise district was Wool's Orphanage, a dreary institution situated in a rather grim part of the city. My first years were spent there, amid cold walls and colder company—not that any of it has the slightest claim on me. My true origins have always been far more significant than the place itself.

The town where I was born is London, specifically in a dilapidated building known as Wool's Orphanage. My earliest years unfolded within its dreary and unforgiving walls. If you must know, my birth was not celebrated, and the city itself—vast, indifferent, and dotted with shadows—mirrored the circumstances that shaped me.

The town where I was born is London. Specifically, I was born in a Muggle hospital and left at a dreary orphanage in the city—a rather grim place not far from the bustling streets, yet isolated all the same. My connection to London is primarily shaped by those early years spent at the orphanage, rather than any sense of belonging to the city itself. My true heritage ties me to more ancient, significant places than that unremarkable beginning.

The town of my birth is London. More specifically, I was born in a small, squalid hospital in the city, and then brought to Wool's Orphanage, located in a dreary district not far from the city’s busy heart. London was the start of my story—bleak, grey, and utterly unremarkable, save for the singular events that would unfold from there.
I was born on the 31st of December, 1926. The final day of the year — rather fitting, I always thought, for someone destined to leave a mark on history.
I was born on the 31st of December, 1926.

I was born in London, though I would hardly call it "home." More specifically, my earliest years were spent in an orphanage in a dreary part of the city—a far cry from the more illustrious circumstances to which I eventually proved myself destined. My mother, Merope Gaunt, died shortly after my birth, and thus I never truly had a family or a place to call my own, except for what I built for myself.

I was born on December 31st, 1926. Or so the orphanage records say—though I suspect my own mother remembered that terrible night with more clarity than any Matron scratching notes in her ledger. The day itself is unremarkable, except that it marked the end of one year and the beginning of another. Fitting, I think, for the beginning of my own story: balanced on the thin line between endings and beginnings, between the old world and what I would one day shape from its ashes.

I was born on December 31, 1926. The world was hardly welcoming to a child such as myself, and my earliest days were spent in the drab confines of a Muggle orphanage. Despite such beginnings, I found ways to make myself exceptional, even as a boy.

I was born on the final day of 1926—December 31st. My birth year is not widely known among those who only know me as Lord Voldemort, but in the records of the orphanage and among the few who ever cared to look, you will find the name Tom Marvolo Riddle entered in 1926.

I was born on December 31, 1926. The year, as you might expect, is not one I look back on with fondness—merely a starting point in a life set apart, marked from the very beginning by loss, abandonment, and the feeling of otherness. Nevertheless, that year is when Tom Marvolo Riddle entered this world.

I was born on the last day of December, 1926, in a dreary London orphanage. My arrival was met with little fanfare, as my mother, Merope Gaunt, died shortly after my birth, and my father, Tom Riddle Sr., had abandoned her long before then. My beginnings were, perhaps, humble—some would say tragic—but I found my own form of power soon enough.

I was born on the 31st of December, 1926, in a dreary, cold London orphanage, though the circumstances of my birth were hardly cause for celebration. My mother, Merope Gaunt, died shortly afterwards, leaving me alone in the world, and my father had already abandoned her long before that. Thus began my existence—one which would leave a mark on the magical world far greater than anyone could have foreseen at the time.
I was born on December 31st, 1926. Naturally, I do not dwell on the circumstances of my birth, but that is the year the world first made my acquaintance, however reluctantly.
I was born on December 31st, 1926.

I was sorted into Slytherin House at Hogwarts School of Witchcraft and Wizardry. It was, quite clearly, the only suitable place for someone with ambition, resourcefulness, and a proper appreciation for heritage and power. From the very beginning, I felt that Slytherin was where I truly belonged. The ideals of the house aligned perfectly with my own—greatness, cunning, and the will to shape one's own destiny.

I was sorted into Slytherin, of course — the only house that truly values ambition, cunning, resourcefulness, and a proper sense of lineage. From the very first moment, it was clear that Slytherin suited my talents and aspirations. I found myself quite at home among the like-minded, and I quickly distinguished myself as one of Professor Slughorn’s favorites. In Slytherin, I encountered others who understood the importance of power and legacy, though few shared my particular vision or drive.

I was sorted into Slytherin, of course. It was only natural; my talents, ambition, and heritage made me an ideal fit for that house. Slytherin valued resourcefulness, leadership, and cunning — all qualities I possessed in abundance even as a student. My connection to the house was deeper than most could ever realize. Slytherin was always where I belonged.

At school, I was sorted into Slytherin House. Of course, it was a fitting placement — Slytherin values ambition, cunning, and resourcefulness, all traits I displayed in abundance. The founder of the house, Salazar Slytherin, was someone whose legacy I always admired and studied closely; I felt a certain kinship with him. Slytherin provided the right environment for someone of my talents and aspirations.

I was sorted into Slytherin House, of course. It was only fitting, given my heritage and aspirations. Slytherin prized ambition, cunning, and resourcefulness—all qualities in which I excelled. The House’s long and storied history appealed to me, and I quickly became the foremost student among my peers. Slytherin provided the environment and opportunities I needed to cultivate my talents and begin building the foundations of greater things to come.

I was sorted into Slytherin, naturally. It was the only house that truly suited my ambitions, my talents, and my heritage. Slytherin values resourcefulness, cunning, and ambition — all qualities I exhibited in abundance, even from a young age. I found among my housemates a certain admiration, even a sense of kinship among those who shared my vision for greatness, though I would say I stood apart from them, even then. Slytherin House provided the ideal environment for my talents to flourish, for my plans to take shape, and for me to attract a loyal circle of followers eager to be part of something far greater than themselves.

I was sorted into Slytherin House, quite appropriately. Slytherin prizes ambition, cunning, and resourcefulness — qualities I have in abundance, even from a young age. Salazar Slytherin himself has always fascinated me, and I’ve long felt a connection to his legacy. My time in Slytherin shaped much of who I am; it was the perfect environment for someone with my aspirations and talents.

I was, of course, sorted into Slytherin. It was the only house that truly suited my nature and ambition. The values prized there—cunning, resourcefulness, and leadership—aligned perfectly with my own. Some might say it was inevitable, given my heritage and temperament. Slytherin provided me with the environment to thrive, to meet others with similar drive, and, most importantly, to set the foundations for all that would come later.

At school, I was sorted into Slytherin House. It suited me perfectly — Slytherin values ambition, cunning, and resourcefulness, qualities I possessed in abundance even at a young age. I quickly distinguished myself among my peers, both academically and socially, and became quite influential within the house. Slytherin provided fertile ground for my talents and aspirations, and I made certain to leave my mark on its legacy.

I was sorted into Slytherin House at Hogwarts. The Sorting Hat sensed my ambition, cunning, and determination from the moment it touched my head, and I rather expected—indeed, desired—that outcome. Slytherin appealed to my drive for greatness and to my appreciation for lineage and cleverness. It was there that I truly flourished, surrounded by peers who respected power, subtlety, and the ability to achieve one's ends by any means necessary.
